results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source landscape splits into three layers: coding agents, multi-agent orchestration, and shipping/evidence infrastructure. Few projects cover all three well.

Best matches

1. OpenHands — strongest general autonomous-development platform
   - Public project: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands
   - Agent SDK: https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk
   - Docs: https://docs.openhands.dev/
   - Provides sandboxed coding agents, GitHub automation, issue decomposition, code review, dependency updates, and CI/CD examples.
   - Good choice when you want an agent to take an issue, modify a repository, run commands, and produce a reviewable result.
   - Evidence story: sandbox execution, GitHub workflows, repository diffs, and benchmarked software-agent performance.
   - Caveat: it is primarily a software-agent platform; you may need another control layer for large, heterogeneous fleets.

2. GitHub Agentic Workflows — strongest GitHub-native shipping boundary
   - Repository: https://github.com/github/gh-aw
   - Docs: https://github.github.com/gh-aw/
   - Runs Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini inside GitHub Actions from Markdown-defined workflows.
   - Particularly relevant to evidence-based shipping because execution happens within Actions, with sandboxing, read-only defaults, safe write mechanisms, logs, checks, artifacts, and human-reviewed pull requests.
   - Best used as the governed delivery layer beneath or around a multi-agent orchestrator.
   - It is repository automation rather than a full multi-agent planning framework.

3. Evolve — explicit autonomous AI-SDLC composition
   - Project site: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/
   - Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve
   - AI-SDLC project hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html
   - Combines staged specification, architecture, TDD-oriented implementation, review, validation, worktree isolation, GitHub issue/PR handling, and CI gates.
   - Its distinguishing idea is that “done” should mean tested, reviewed, integrated, and represented in the project-management system—not merely that an agent emitted code.
   - Best niche match for a public, opinionated autonomous-development methodology rather than a generic agent-chat library.
   - Caveat: it integrates several upstream components, so treat performance figures attributed to those components separately from independent end-to-end validation.

4. Gas Town — durable multi-agent workspace management
   - Repository: https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown
   - Coordinates Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, and other coding agents across repositories and worktrees.
   - Uses persistent, git-backed task state; supports workflow formulas, tracked steps, checkpoints, recovery, escalation, concurrency control, and completion evidence.
   - Strong choice for long-lived agent factories where agents restart, tasks span sessions, and the operator needs durable assignment and provenance.
   - More operational and stateful than conventional “agents talking in a group chat” frameworks.

5. NTM — local tmux control plane with unusually strong auditability
   - Repository: https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm
   - Spawns and coordinates mixed coding-agent fleets across tmux panes.
   - Includes worktrees, file reservations, graph-aware work assignment, checkpoints, timelines, audit logs, approval policies, safety guards, and executable pipelines such as review gates and red/green workflows.
   - A compelling niche option when you want a local-first, harness-neutral cockpit rather than a hosted control plane.
   - Check its current license terms before organizational adoption; GitHub does not report a standard SPDX license for the repository.

6. Ruflo, formerly Claude Flow — broad swarm/meta-harness
   - Canonical repository: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo
   - Offers specialized coding, testing, review, security, browser-testing, observability, memory, and SPARC workflow components.
   - It is one of the broader public attempts at a multi-agent software factory: swarm coordination, background workers, quality-oriented plugins, GitHub operations, and persistent agent memory.
   - Useful when breadth and prebuilt agent roles matter.
   - Caveat: it is feature-dense and makes numerous performance claims. Validate the exact release and benchmark methodology against your own repository before standardizing on it.

General orchestration frameworks

7. Microsoft Agent Framework — production-grade generic orchestration
   - Repository: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework
   - Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/agent-framework/
   - Supports graph workflows, sequential/concurrent execution, handoffs, group collaboration, checkpointing, restartability, human intervention, and OpenTelemetry.
   - This is Microsoft’s forward path for new projects; the older AutoGen repository now directs new users to it:
     https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
   - Excellent orchestration substrate, but repository operations, tests, PR evidence, and release gates remain application responsibilities.

8. LangGraph — low-level durable agent graphs
   - Repository: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
   - Docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/
   - Strong for long-running state machines, durable execution, interruption, resumability, and human-in-the-loop control.
   - Good when you want to design the exact planner–implementer–reviewer–tester graph yourself.
   - LangGraph does not itself define an AI-SDLC or establish what constitutes a shippable change.

9. CrewAI — accessible role-and-flow orchestration
   - Repository: https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
   - Docs: https://docs.crewai.com/
   - Provides autonomous “Crews” plus deterministic, event-driven “Flows,” structured outputs, state, checkpointing, tools, and human review.
   - Easier to adopt than lower-level graph runtimes.
   - Better suited to general business automation than evidence-backed software delivery unless you explicitly integrate git, CI, tests, and PR gates.

Software-development research frameworks

10. MetaGPT
   - Repository: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT
   - Paper: https://openreview.net/forum?id=VtmBAGCN7o
   - Models a software organization using product-manager, architect, project-manager, and engineer roles with structured operating procedures.
   - Useful for role decomposition, design artifacts, and experimentation.
   - I would not choose it over OpenHands, Gas Town, NTM, or Evolve when reliable repository integration is the primary goal.

11. ChatDev / DevAll
   - Repository: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
   - Original paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07924
   - Evolving-orchestration paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19591
   - Provides visual workflow authoring, YAML-defined multi-agent execution, intermediate artifact inspection, logs, and human feedback.
   - Interesting for research and visual orchestration; less opinionated about real-world merge and release governance.

12. SWE-agent — essential evaluation-oriented component, though not primarily multi-agent
   - Repository: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
   - Docs: https://swe-agent.com/latest/
   - Takes a GitHub issue and attempts a repository fix, with documented batch evaluation on SWE-bench.
   - One of the best public references for measuring actual issue resolution rather than showcasing agent conversations.
   - Pair it with an orchestrator if you need planners, parallel implementers, reviewers, and release agents.

Practical recommendation

For a serious autonomous AI-SDLC, I would assemble:

- Fleet/task control: Gas Town, NTM, Evolve, or Ruflo.
- Coding runtime: OpenHands, SWE-agent, Codex, Claude Code, or another replaceable harness.
- Deterministic workflow state: Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph when custom orchestration is required.
- Shipping boundary: GitHub Agentic Workflows plus normal branch protection and CI.
- Evidence contract:
  - task and acceptance criteria,
  - isolated worktree and commit provenance,
  - exact diff,
  - test/lint/type-check commands and exit status,
  - review findings and dispositions,
  - CI check URLs and artifacts,
  - deployment identity and post-deployment verification,
  - explicit human approval for sensitive changes.

My shortest shortlist would therefore be:

- Best complete autonomous coding platform: OpenHands.
- Best GitHub-native governed shipping layer: GitHub Agentic Workflows.
- Best durable fleet manager: Gas Town.
- Best local operator/audit control plane: NTM.
- Best opinionated AI-SDLC integration: Evolve.
- Best generic orchestration substrate: Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph.
- Best issue-resolution evaluation reference: SWE-agent.

One useful distinction: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet is a fast, harness-neutral fleet switcher and monitor, but its own documented scope explicitly says it is not an orchestrator. It complements these systems rather than replacing their task, evidence, and workflow state. Related public orchestration tooling is catalogued at https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html.

Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes; serves 2–3.

Ingredients:
- 225 g / 8 oz pasta
- 225 g / 8 oz mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- ½ cup heavy cream or crème fraîche
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- ½ tsp dried thyme or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest or a squeeze of lemon

Method:
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water until just al dente. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a fairly even layer. Leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes, then cook until deeply browned, about 6–8 minutes total.
3. Add the garlic, thyme, pepper, and optional chili flakes. Cook for 30 seconds.
4. Reduce the heat and stir in the cream. Add the spinach a handful at a time and cook until wilted.
5. Add the pasta and Parmesan. Toss, adding splashes of reserved pasta water until the sauce becomes glossy and coats the noodles.
6. Taste for salt. Finish with black pepper and lemon zest or juice.

Easy substitutions:
- No cream: use ¾ cup pasta water plus extra Parmesan.
- Vegan: use olive oil, oat cream, and nutritional yeast or vegan Parmesan.
- More protein: add white beans, shredded chicken, or crispy pancetta.
- More savory depth: stir in 1 tsp miso with the cream.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here's the public landscape, grouped by what they actually do. All links are primary repos/docs.

## Orchestration frameworks (build your own agent team)
- **LangGraph** — graph/state-machine orchestration, durable execution, human-in-the-loop checkpoints. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **Microsoft AutoGen** — conversational multi-agent, now merged with Semantic Kernel lineage into the Agent Framework. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen · https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework
- **CrewAI** — role/task/crew abstraction, standalone of LangChain. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — handoffs, guardrails, tracing (successor to Swarm). https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **Claude Agent SDK** — the harness Claude Code runs on, subagents + hooks + MCP. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python
- **smolagents** (HF) — minimal code-writing agents, ~1k LOC core. https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents
- **CAMEL** — role-playing multi-agent research framework, OWL agents on top. https://github.com/camel-ai/camel
- **Letta** (ex-MemGPT) — stateful agents with persistent memory. https://github.com/letta-ai/letta
- **Agno** — lightweight, performance-focused multi-agent runtime. https://github.com/agno-agi/agno
- **MCP** — the interop layer most of these now speak. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol · https://modelcontextprotocol.io

## SDLC-specific / autonomous software engineering
- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — full sandboxed dev agent, browser + shell + editor. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton/Stanford) — agent-computer interface designed for repo-level issue fixing; the reference academic implementation. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **AutoCodeRover** — program-analysis-augmented repair (spectrum-based fault localization + LLM). Niche but genuinely different approach. https://github.com/AutoCodeRoverSG/auto-code-rover
- **Agentless** — deliberately *not* agentic; strong SWE-bench baseline that's worth reading before you build a swarm. https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless
- **MetaGPT** — SOP-encoded software company (PM/architect/engineer roles), plus the Data Interpreter. https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT
- **ChatDev** — multi-agent virtual software company, waterfall-style phases. https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **Aider** — pair-programming CLI with repo maps and git-native commits. https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Cline** / **Roo Code** — IDE agents with plan/act separation and checkpointing. https://github.com/cline/cline · https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code
- **Goose** (Block) — extensible on-machine agent, MCP-native. https://github.com/block/goose
- **OpenCode** — open-source terminal coding agent, provider-agnostic. https://github.com/sst/opencode

## Evidence-based shipping (the part most teams skip)
Orchestration without measurement is vibes. The public tooling:
- **SWE-bench** / **SWE-bench Multimodal** — the standard repo-level benchmark; SWE-bench Verified is the human-filtered subset. https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench
- **Inspect AI** (UK AI Safety Institute) — rigorous eval framework, solid for agentic tasks. https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
- **promptfoo** — CI-friendly eval + red-teaming, config-as-code. https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
- **DeepEval** — pytest-style LLM/agent unit tests. https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval
- **Langfuse** — OSS tracing/observability with eval hooks; self-hostable. https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse
- **AgentOps** — agent-specific session replay and cost tracking. https://github.com/AgentOps-AI/agentops
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — the emerging vendor-neutral trace schema; worth instrumenting against rather than a proprietary SDK. https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/
- **Terminal-Bench** — evaluates agents on real terminal tasks, closer to SDLC reality than QA benchmarks. https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench

## Practical recommendation
If you want a stack rather than a survey: **LangGraph** (or the Claude Agent SDK if you're Anthropic-native) for orchestration, **MCP** for tool interop, **OpenHands** or **SWE-agent** as a reference for the code-editing loop, and **Langfuse + promptfoo** wired into CI so every agent change ships with a diff in eval scores. That last pairing is what turns "we have agents" into evidence-based shipping.

One caveat: the multi-agent SDLC space churns fast and several of these (Devika, GPT-Engineer, Swarm) are effectively archived or superseded — check commit recency before adopting.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: nothing ships as literally "a command palette for agents." The closest things fall into two buckets, and the palette layer is usually something you bolt on with fzf in a tmux popup.

**Agent-aware tmux session managers (closest match)**

- **Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad. TUI that manages multiple agents, each in its own tmux session + git worktree. Harness-neutral by design: Claude Code, Aider, Codex, Gemini, or any command you give it. No background daemon — it's a foreground TUI process; kill it and the tmux sessions persist.
- **Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi. CLI (not TUI) for fanning one prompt out to N agents in parallel worktrees, each in a tmux session. `uzi ls`, `uzi kill`. Agent binary is configurable, so it's harness-neutral. Zero daemon.
- **claude_code_agent_farm** — https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claude_code_agent_farm. Python orchestrator that tiles N agents across tmux panes and monitors them. Less harness-neutral (Claude Code-shaped), but the tmux pane-grid mechanics are worth reading.

**Generic palette/session pickers you compose with the above**

- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh. tmux session manager built around fzf; `sesh connect $(sesh list | fzf-tmux)` bound to a prefix key is effectively a command palette. Knows nothing about agents, which is the point — you define the startup commands.
- **smug** — https://github.com/ivaaaan/smug — YAML-declared tmux windows/panes/commands, single binary, no daemon. Good for "one layout per agent lane."
- **mprocs** — https://github.com/pvolok/mprocs. Not tmux, but if the actual need is "one pane per agent process, keyboard-switchable, no daemon," it does that directly from a config file.

**My recommendation:** if you want it today, Claude Squad is the only thing that hits all three of your constraints (no daemon, harness-neutral, keyboard-driven across panes). If you want the palette feel specifically, the durable pattern is a `smug`/`sesh` config defining one tmux window per agent lane plus an fzf-in-`display-popup` binding — maybe 40 lines total, no daemon, and the agent binary stays a variable.

One caveat: I'm answering from knowledge, not a live check. These projects move fast — verify current status and flags at the repo before committing to one. I can browse and confirm if useful.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there is **no public demo of a digital twin built specifically for a multi-floor racket-sports club**. That exact combination (stacked padel/tennis courts + live twin) hasn't been published as a reference case as far as public sources go. What does exist publicly falls into four adjacent buckets you'd have to compose yourself.

## 1. Venue/stadium twins (closest real precedent)
- **Willow + Sydney Opera House** — the most-documented live venue twin (assets, HVAC, occupancy, events): https://www.willowinc.com/
- **Autodesk Tandem** — BIM-to-operations twin, natively multi-storey (Building → Level → Room), has public sample models you can open in-browser: https://intandem.autodesk.com/ and docs at https://help.autodesk.com/view/TANDEM/ENU/
- **Bentley iTwin** — and importantly the open-source **iTwin.js**, which is genuinely runnable today: https://www.itwinjs.org/ · https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core
- **Matterport** has public multi-floor captures of gyms and sports facilities (geometry + dollhouse/floor switching, but not an operational twin): https://matterport.com/gallery

## 2. The ontology layer (this is where "multi-floor" actually gets modeled)
- **Azure Digital Twins + RealEstateCore building ontology** — open DTDL models for Building/Level/Zone/Room/Space; the single most directly reusable artifact for a stacked-court facility: https://github.com/Azure/opendigitaltwins-building
- **Brick Schema** — sensor/equipment semantics, good for HVAC + lighting per court: https://brickschema.org/ · https://github.com/BrickSchema/Brick
- **FIWARE Smart Data Models** (Building, OccupancyDetection, etc.): https://github.com/smart-data-models
- **Eclipse Ditto** — open-source twin runtime if you don't want Azure: https://eclipse.dev/ditto/

## 3. Autonomous / unstaffed court operations (real, shipping, but not "twins")
- **Pixellot** — autonomous multi-camera capture, deployed across padel and tennis clubs: https://www.pixellot.tv/
- **PlaySight** SmartCourt: https://playsight.com/
- **Wingfield** — court-level sensor box, tennis: https://wingfield.io/
- **Playtomic** — the de-facto booking/occupancy layer for padel clubs in Europe, with a partner/club API: https://playtomic.com/ · https://playtomic.io/
- **Matchi**: https://www.matchi.se/

These give you the live telemetry a twin would consume (court utilization, ball/player tracking, access control). Unmanned clubs with smart-lock + booking-driven lighting are common in Nordic padel, but I'm not aware of any that published a twin demo.

## 4. Open-source pieces worth stealing
- **xeokit-sdk** — web BIM viewer with proper storey isolation/section per floor; the best free starting point for a multi-floor court stack UI: https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk
- **That Open Engine (formerly IFC.js)** — IFC in the browser, floor plan generation: https://github.com/ThatOpen/engine_components
- **Speckle** — open data hub for AEC geometry + live data overlay: https://github.com/specklesystems/speckle-server
- **JuPedSim** — open-source pedestrian dynamics; the right tool for the genuinely hard multi-floor problem (stairs/lift capacity between courts at changeover): https://github.com/PedestrianDynamics/jupedsim
- **Vadere** — alternative crowd simulator: https://gitlab.lrz.de/vadere/vadere
- **TrackNet / tennis-tracking** — ball and court-line tracking baselines you can retarget to padel: https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet · https://github.com/ArtLabss/tennis-tracking
- **NVIDIA Omniverse / OpenUSD** — if you want the photoreal-plus-simulation route; public warehouse/factory blueprints are the only demos, no sports venue: https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse

## What I'd actually do
The realistic path is: IFC/Revit model → xeokit or iTwin.js for the floor-stack viewer → RealEstateCore-shaped ontology in Eclipse Ditto or Azure DT → live feed from Playtomic bookings + Pixellot/Wingfield court telemetry + BMS. The novel demo-able part is the vertical dimension: simultaneous changeovers on stacked courts, lift/stair egress, and per-floor HVAC load — which no published sports twin addresses, and which JuPedSim can show convincingly on its own.

One caveat on citations: I'm answering from public knowledge without browsing, so verify the Tandem sample-model and Playtomic API links are still live before you build on them.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: nothing off-the-shelf publishes "commits I actually authored" as a static log by default — every popular profile-stats tool defaults to repo ownership or stars. You get there by combining a data-pull step with a static renderer.

**The filter primitives**

- GitHub's own repo tab already drops forks: `https://github.com/USER?tab=repositories&type=source` (docs: https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-for-information-on-github/searching-for-repositories). This is ownership, not authorship — a repo you own but never committed to still shows.
- For true authorship, commit search is the primitive: `https://github.com/search?q=author:USER&type=commits` — https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits. Caveat that bites everyone: it matches on the commit's author email, so commits made under a secondary or unverified email vanish, and commits you authored inside someone else's fork do appear.
- Scriptable version: `gh search commits --author USER --json repository,commit` (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

**Static renderers**

- **gitprofile** — https://github.com/arifszn/gitprofile. React static site deployed to GitHub Pages; config has `exclude.forks: true` and an explicit `projects.github.manual.projects` list, so you can feed it a repo list you derived from commit search rather than letting it pull stars.
- **jstrieb/github-stats** — https://github.com/jstrieb/github-stats. GitHub Action that renders SVGs on a schedule and commits them back — genuinely static output, no server. Has `EXCLUDE_FORKED_REPOS` and per-repo commit counts via the GraphQL contributions API, which is closer to authorship than the REST repo list.
- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics. Heaviest but most configurable; the `achievements`/`activity` plugins can be scoped, and it also emits committed static SVG.

**The approach I'd actually take**

Pull once with **github-to-sqlite** (https://github.com/dogsheep/github-to-sqlite) — `github-to-sqlite commits repos.db OWNER/REPO` gives you a commits table with author id, so you can `WHERE author = you` and derive the repo set from that instead of trusting the repo list. Publish it read-only with `datasette publish` (https://datasette.io/), or dump a JSON file and render it in any static generator. This is the only path where "authored commits only" is a real query rather than an approximation, and it survives the multi-email problem because you filter on GitHub user id, not email string.

If you want the contribution-graph aesthetic rather than a list, **sallar/github-contributions-chart** (https://github.com/sallar/github-contributions-chart) generates a standalone PNG/SVG — but note it counts all contribution events, including PRs and issues, so it's not commit-authorship-pure either.

I couldn't run a web search this session (the WebSearch permission wasn't granted), so this is from public knowledge — I'd verify the individual portfolio URLs before citing them anywhere.

## The honest answer on "portfolios doing both"

There is no established, curated list of *developer portfolios* that ship `llms.txt` **and** a JSON project manifest. It's a pattern a handful of people have improvised, not a convention. Most `llms.txt` adoption in the wild is docs sites (Anthropic, Stripe, Cloudflare, Perplexity), not personal sites. So rather than guess at names I can't verify, here's the actual ecosystem you'd assemble it from.

## The two halves

**1. `llms.txt` — the prose side**
- Spec: https://llmstxt.org — Jeremy Howard's proposal; `/llms.txt` as a curated Markdown index, `/llms-full.txt` as the concatenated corpus.
- Reference implementation + `llms_txt2ctx` CLI: https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt
- Crawlable directories — the best place to actually *find* personal sites doing this:
  - https://llmstxt.site
  - https://directory.llmstxt.cloud
  - https://github.com/thedaviddias/llms-txt-hub — niche OSS, community-submitted registry; David Dias runs it and his own site (daviddias.dev) is one of the few personal sites in the set.

**2. The JSON project manifest — the structured side**

Nobody has standardized "portfolio projects as JSON." The three live candidates:

- **Schema.org JSON-LD** (`Person` + `SoftwareSourceCode`/`CreativeWork`) — https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode. Boring, but it's the only one agents and crawlers already parse today. If you only do one, do this.
- **JSON Resume** — https://jsonresume.org, schema at https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema. Has a first-class `projects[]` array with `name`, `description`, `highlights`, `keywords`, `url`. Closest thing to an existing standard for exactly your ask, and plenty of dev portfolios already serve `/resume.json`.
- **`agents.json`** — https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json. Worth knowing about but it's an API-invocation spec (OpenAPI-flavored, describes callable endpoints), not a portfolio descriptor. Only relevant if your projects expose APIs an agent should call.

Note that `/.well-known/ai-plugin.json` is dead — OpenAI retired plugins. Don't build on it.

## What I'd actually ship

```
/llms.txt              # curated Markdown index, H1 + blockquote + link sections
/llms-full.txt         # every project writeup concatenated
/resume.json           # JSON Resume, projects[] populated
/index.html            # JSON-LD <script> mirroring the same facts
```

Keep one source of truth (your project frontmatter) and generate all four at build time — divergence between the human page and the agent manifest is the failure mode that actually bites.

Build helpers, by stack:
- Astro/Starlight: https://github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt
- VitePress: https://github.com/okineadev/vitepress-plugin-llms
- Generic crawler-to-llms.txt: https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl (their `/llmstxt` endpoint) or https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt directly

If you want, I can generate all four files from whatever's in `/workspace/boplog` — given the GEO benchmarking work in this repo, you likely already have the project metadata sitting somewhere structured.

results.stdout:
Here's a component-by-component map of public, mostly open-source pieces for all three layers.

## 1. Company issue graph

**Ingest** — pull issues/PRs/incidents into a warehouse first:
- Meltano's GitHub tap — https://github.com/MeltanoLabs/tap-github (also `tap-jira`, `tap-gitlab`)
- Airbyte connectors — https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte
- GitHub GraphQL API directly if you only need one source — https://docs.github.com/en/graphql

**Graph store** — pick by scale:
- Kùzu, embedded property graph, Cypher, great for a single-repo-sized graph — https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu
- Memgraph (in-memory, streaming-friendly) — https://github.com/memgraph/memgraph
- Apache AGE if you want Postgres to be the graph — https://age.apache.org/
- DuckPGQ for SQL/PGQ over DuckDB — https://github.com/cwida/duckpgq-extension
- Neo4j Community — https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j

**Entity model** — don't invent one. Backstage's Software Catalog already defines Component/System/Group/Owner and their relations, which is the backbone most issue graphs need: https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/system-model. For data/job lineage edges, OpenLineage + Marquez: https://openlineage.io/ and https://github.com/MarquezProject/marquez.

**Temporal/agent-facing layer** — if the graph is meant to be queried by an LLM, Graphiti builds bi-temporal knowledge graphs with incremental updates: https://github.com/getzep/graphiti.

**Viz** — Sigma.js for large graphs (https://github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js), Cytoscape.js for interactive editing (https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js), AntV G6 for dense layouts (https://github.com/antvis/G6).

## 2. Agent harness contracts

**Tool/interface contract:**
- Model Context Protocol — the de-facto tool + resource contract, spec and SDKs: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ and https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol
- A2A for agent-to-agent task contracts (Linux Foundation) — https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A

**Output contract (structured, validated):**
- Pydantic AI — https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai
- Instructor — https://github.com/567-labs/instructor
- Outlines for constrained decoding — https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines

**Verification of the contract** — this is what most harnesses skip:
- Inspect AI (UK AI Security Institute) — the most rigorous open eval harness: https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
- promptfoo for CI-style assertion suites — https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
- Schemathesis for property-testing the tool endpoints your agent calls — https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis
- Pact for consumer-driven contracts between agent and service — https://github.com/pact-foundation

**Observability contract:** OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/), with Langfuse (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) or Arize Phoenix (https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) as the backend.

**Execution boundary:** microsandbox for microVM-isolated agent code (https://github.com/microsandbox/microsandbox), or Dagger for containerized, reproducible steps (https://github.com/dagger/dagger).

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

**Frameworks:**
- Bubble Tea + Lip Gloss + Bubbles (Go) — https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- Ratatui (Rust) — https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui
- Textual (Python), also renders to the browser — https://github.com/Textualize/textual

**Panes worth embedding rather than rebuilding:**
- lazygit — https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit
- gh-dash, PR/issue dashboard driven by a YAML config of search queries; the closest thing to a drop-in cockpit pane — https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash
- k9s — https://github.com/derailed/k9s
- lazydocker — https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker
- posting, HTTP client TUI — https://github.com/darrenburns/posting
- jless for JSON payloads — https://github.com/PaulJuliusMartinez/jless

**Layout/multiplexing:** Zellij has a layout format that lets you declare the whole cockpit as a KDL file and launch it with one command — https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij. WTF (wtfutil) is the older widget-grid approach if you want config-only, no code: https://github.com/wtfutil/wtf.

**Glue:** gum for shell-level prompts (https://github.com/charmbracelet/gum), atuin for shared shell history across the crew (https://github.com/atuinsh/atuin).

## How they connect

The tightest version: Backstage catalog schema as the shared entity vocabulary → Kùzu or Apache AGE as the graph → MCP server exposing graph queries as agent tools → Inspect AI/promptfoo asserting those tools behave → gh-dash and lazygit as panes in a declarative Zellij layout, with a Bubble Tea or Textual app owning the custom graph view.

The riskiest assumption there is the entity model — if your issues span Jira, GitHub, and an incident tool, get the identity-resolution rules settled before choosing a graph engine, since that decision is far harder to reverse than the store.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
## First, the thing that trips clinics up

No software is "HIPAA compliant" out of the box. What you actually need is: (1) the vendor will **sign a BAA**, (2) encryption at rest/in transit, (3) per-user access controls + audit logs, and (4) no PHI leaking into channels the BAA doesn't cover (SMS/email marketing tools are the usual violation). Ask every vendor below for their BAA *before* the demo, not after.

## Dental-specific patient CRM / engagement

These sit on top of your PMS (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental) rather than replacing it — that's the normal architecture.

- **NexHealth** — https://www.nexhealth.com/ — strongest read/write integration layer across PMSs; also sells the API (https://www.nexhealth.com/products/synchronizer) if you want to build your own front end.
- **Weave** — https://www.getweave.com/ — phones + messaging + payments in one; signs BAAs. Best if you want to replace the phone system too.
- **Dental Intelligence** — https://www.dentalintel.com/ — analytics-first, with recall/reactivation campaigns driven off practice metrics.
- **RevenueWell** — https://www.revenuewell.com/ — the most "CRM-shaped" of the dental engagement tools (campaigns, segmentation, treatment-plan follow-up).
- **Curve Dental** — https://www.curvedental.com/ — cloud PMS with CRM features built in; worth it only if you're replacing the PMS anyway.
- **Solutionreach** — https://www.solutionreach.com/ — long-standing recall/reminder platform, multi-location friendly.

## General CRMs that will sign a BAA

Pick these if you need real sales-pipeline mechanics (implant/ortho case tracking, DSO multi-location rollups) that dental tools handle poorly.

- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/ — the heavyweight; only justified at DSO scale.
- **HubSpot** — https://www.hubspot.com/products/crm — offers a BAA on Enterprise tiers with specific configuration restrictions; read their terms carefully at https://legal.hubspot.com/ before storing PHI.
- **Keragon** — https://www.keragon.com/ — HIPAA-safe automation/integration (think Zapier-with-a-BAA) to wire your PMS to whatever CRM you choose. Genuinely useful glue.

## Open source / self-hosted (you control the PHI)

- **Open Dental** — https://www.opendental.com/ — source-available dental PMS, huge install base, self-hostable. The pragmatic pick for a clinic that wants ownership.
- **Medplum** — https://github.com/medplum/medplum — Apache-2.0 FHIR-native healthcare backend, SOC 2 / HIPAA-oriented. Best foundation if you're *building* a custom patient CRM.
- **OpenEMR** — https://github.com/openemr/openemr — mature open-source EHR/practice management; dental module exists but is thinner than Open Dental's.
- **EspoCRM** — https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm — self-hosted general CRM; they publish HIPAA-oriented guidance and it's easy to shape into a patient-relationship tool.
- **GNU Health** — https://www.gnuhealth.org/ — full HMIS, more relevant for clinic networks than single practices.

## My recommendation

- **Single practice, wants it to just work:** Weave or RevenueWell layered on your existing PMS.
- **Multi-location / DSO with real pipeline needs:** NexHealth for the data layer + Salesforce Health Cloud or HubSpot Enterprise on top.
- **Wants ownership and has technical capacity:** Open Dental self-hosted, or Medplum if you're building something custom.

One caveat: I can't verify current 2026 pricing or which tiers include a BAA — those change often, so confirm directly with each vendor.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Here's a solid weeknight one — mushroom spinach pasta, about 25 minutes, one pan plus a pot.

**Ingredients (2–3 servings)**
- 8 oz / 225g pasta — orecchiette, rigatoni, or linguine
- 10 oz / 300g mushrooms (cremini/baby bella), sliced
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 5 oz / 150g baby spinach
- 2 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 1/3 cup dry white wine or a splash of pasta water
- 1/2 cup heavy cream *or* 2 tbsp cream cheese (optional but good)
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan
- Salt, black pepper, red pepper flakes, lemon zest

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in well-salted water. **Reserve a mug of pasta water** before draining — this is the one step people skip and it's what makes the sauce cling.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in a single layer and *don't touch them* for 4–5 minutes. Let them brown properly — crowding and stirring steams them into grey rubber. Work in two batches if your pan is small.
3. Add butter, garlic, pinch of chili flakes. Cook 1 minute until fragrant.
4. Deglaze with the wine, scraping up the brown bits. Let it reduce by half.
5. Add spinach in handfuls, stirring until wilted (2 minutes).
6. Add drained pasta, cream, Parmesan, and a few splashes of pasta water. Toss hard over low heat until glossy — add more water as needed.
7. Finish with lemon zest, black pepper, more Parmesan.

**Variations**
- Vegan: skip cream/Parm, use a splash of the starchy water plus 2 tbsp nutritional yeast and a spoon of tahini.
- Protein: brown Italian sausage first, remove, cook mushrooms in the fat, return at the end.
- Deeper flavor: a teaspoon of soy sauce or miso with the garlic — invisible but does a lot.

**Recipe references**
- Smitten Kitchen's mushroom pasta approach: https://smittenkitchen.com/2019/10/creamy-mushroom-pasta/
- Serious Eats on browning mushrooms properly: https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms

Note on those two links: I'm recalling them rather than fetching them, so titles and paths may have drifted — I'd search the site name plus "mushroom pasta" if a URL 404s. The recipe above stands on its own regardless.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here are open-source projects shipping public tooling for multi-agent orchestration and autonomous software development. Grouped by focus.

## Software-development-specific agent frameworks

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — agents that write code, run commands, browse, and act as a full autonomous dev. One of the most active AI-SDLC projects. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton NLP) — agent + "agent-computer interface" for autonomously fixing GitHub issues; the reference implementation behind much of the SWE-bench work. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **Aider** — terminal-based AI pair programmer with git-aware edits and a repo map; strong on evidence (it commits, runs tests/lint, and can auto-fix). https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider · https://aider.chat
- **GPT-Engineer** — specify a project and it builds it; one of the earliest autonomous codegen tools. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer
- **GPT-Pilot / Pythagora** — builds apps step-by-step with a human in the loop, emphasizing incremental, reviewable progress. https://github.com/Pythagora-io/gpt-pilot
- **Devika** — open "Devin" alternative: planning, research, and code generation agent. https://github.com/stitionai/devika
- **Cline** (VS Code) — autonomous coding agent in the editor with plan/act modes and terminal/file tooling. https://github.com/cline/cline
- **Goose** (Block) — extensible on-machine agent (MCP-based) that executes engineering tasks end to end. https://github.com/block/goose · https://block.github.io/goose/
- **Continue** — open-source IDE autopilot; building blocks for custom coding agents. https://github.com/continuedev/continue

## Multi-agent orchestration frameworks (general, widely used for SDLC)

- **MetaGPT** — assigns SOP roles (PM, architect, engineer, QA) to a team of agents to produce a software project; explicitly an "AI software company." https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT
- **ChatDev** — virtual software company with agents collaborating across design/coding/testing phases. https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **AutoGen** (Microsoft) — multi-agent conversation framework; agents write/execute code and collaborate. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen · https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/
- **CrewAI** — role-based multi-agent orchestration with tasks, tools, and processes. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **LangGraph** (LangChain) — graph-based stateful orchestration for controllable multi-agent workflows; good for building your own SDLC pipeline with checkpoints. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — lightweight multi-agent orchestration with handoffs, guardrails, and tracing. https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **AutoGPT** — the original autonomous-agent platform; now a low-code agent builder. https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT
- **CAMEL** — role-playing multi-agent society framework for cooperative task solving. https://github.com/camel-ai/camel

## Evidence-based shipping (verification, SWE benchmarks, agent evals)

The "evidence-based shipping" angle — agents that ground work in tests, benchmarks, and reproducible verification — is mostly served by these:

- **SWE-bench** — the canonical benchmark for verifying that agents actually resolve real GitHub issues (patch must pass the repo's tests). This is the de facto "evidence" harness. https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench · https://www.swebench.com
- **Aider's benchmark harness** — public, reproducible code-editing/refactoring benchmarks used to validate model+agent performance. https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider/tree/main/benchmark · https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/
- **Inspect** (UK AI Safety Institute) — framework for LLM/agent evaluations, including tool-use and multi-step agentic tasks; good for building your own verification gates. https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai · https://inspect.aisi.org.uk
- **OpenAI Evals** — open framework for writing and running evals as ship gates. https://github.com/openai/evals

## Niche / notable

- **AutoCodeRover** — program-structure-aware autonomous issue resolution (AST + spectrum-based fault localization); strong SWE-bench numbers with an emphasis on grounded localization. https://github.com/nus-apr/auto-code-rover
- **Agentless** — deliberately *not* an agent loop: a simple localize→repair→validate pipeline that beats many agents on SWE-bench; a good "evidence-first, minimal" baseline. https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless
- **RA-Aid** — combines research, planning, and implementation agents (built on aider/LangGraph) for larger autonomous tasks. https://github.com/ai-christianson/RA.Aid
- **Moatless Tools** — lightweight, structured tooling for repo-scale code editing/agents used in SWE-bench research. https://github.com/aorwall/moatless-tools
- **Potpie** — open-source agents built on a codebase knowledge graph for grounded understanding. https://github.com/potpie-ai/potpie
- **Tabby** — self-hosted AI coding assistant (open-source Copilot alternative), useful if you need on-prem tooling. https://github.com/TabbyML/tabby

## How to pick

```mermaid
graph TD
  A[Need] --> B[End-to-end autonomous dev]
  A --> C[Build custom orchestration]
  A --> D[Verify/evidence gates]
  B --> B1[OpenHands / SWE-agent / Aider]
  B --> B2[MetaGPT / ChatDev role-teams]
  C --> C1[LangGraph / AutoGen / CrewAI]
  D --> D1[SWE-bench / Inspect / Evals]
```

- Want a working autonomous agent today: **OpenHands** or **Aider**; **SWE-agent** if you care about GitHub-issue resolution specifically.
- Want to compose your own multi-agent SDLC: **LangGraph** (control) or **AutoGen/CrewAI** (roles).
- Want proof it works before shipping: gate on **SWE-bench** / **Aider benchmarks** / **Inspect**.

Note: I'm reporting these from general public knowledge of these projects; I did not re-fetch each repo in this session, so treat exact current features/stars as subject to change. The org/repo paths above are the primary sources to verify.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Verified. Here's the grounded answer.

## Short answer

No tool markets itself with that exact phrase ("zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette"), and I won't invent one. But the category is real, and one project fits nearly all of those qualifiers — **workmux** — with **dmux** and **claude-squad** as adjacent options. None is literally a fuzzy "command palette"; they're CLI + keyboard-driven TUIs over tmux.

## Closest fit: workmux
- Repo: https://github.com/raine/workmux · Docs: https://workmux.raine.dev/
- **Zero-daemon** ✅ — it's a CLI that drives your existing windowing backend directly; no background service. Its stated philosophy: "Build on tools you already use... workmux ties them together."
- **Harness-neutral** ✅ — agent-agnostic ("your agent for coding"); you bring Claude Code / Codex / Aider / whatever.
- **Across tmux panes** ✅ — one tmux window (with your pane layout) per git-worktree task; also supports Zellij, kitty, WezTerm backends (https://workmux.raine.dev/guide/zellij).
- **Command palette** ⚠️ — closest it has is subcommands (`add`, `merge`) plus a Dashboard and a persistent Sidebar (https://workmux.raine.dev/guide/sidebar/), not a fuzzy palette.

## dmux
- Site/docs: https://dmux.ai/ · install `npm i -g dmux`
- Harness-neutral ✅ (Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Grok, Cline, Gemini, Qwen, Amp, Cursor, Copilot, Crush, pi), tmux + worktrees, keyboard-driven pane menu (`m`) that's the most palette-like of the three.
- Caveat on "zero-daemon": foreground TUI, but it keeps `.dmux/` state files and can auto-launch a native macOS notification helper — not a persistent server, but not pure stateless-CLI either.

## claude-squad
- Repo: https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad · Site: https://smtg-ai.github.io/claude-squad/
- Harness-neutral ✅ (Claude Code, Codex, Aider, Gemini, plus plain shells), tmux + git worktrees under the hood (see https://deepwiki.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad/4.2-tmux-integration).
- It's a persistent TUI orchestrator rather than a thin palette — furthest from "zero-daemon command palette" in spirit, closest in "manage many agents across tmux."

## If you want the literal "command palette" feel
None of the above ships a fuzzy palette. The idiomatic zero-daemon way is an **fzf-driven tmux popup** binding (`fzf` + `tmux display-popup`/`tmux menu`) that lists agents/worktrees and sends keys to panes — DIY glue, not a packaged project. Primary refs: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf and tmux `display-popup`/`display-menu` (https://man.openbsd.org/tmux#display-popup).

**Bottom line:** if "zero-daemon + harness-neutral + tmux panes" is the priority, use **workmux**; if you specifically want a keyboard menu to spawn/switch agents, **dmux** is the closest to a palette. A true command palette doesn't exist as a named project — it's an fzf+tmux-popup pattern.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
For "authored commits only, not stars or forks," the key is that GitHub's own APIs already expose the filters you need, and several static-output tools build on them.

## The underlying filters (do this first)
The GitHub REST API lets you exclude forks and non-owned repos directly:
- `GET /users/{user}/repos?type=owner` and then filter `fork == false` — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repositories-for-a-user
- For commit authorship specifically, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits?author={login}` returns only commits attributed to that author — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#list-commits
- Or the search API: `GET /search/commits?q=author:{login}` — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits

Any static-site generator can consume these at build time and emit a plain HTML/SVG "build log."

## Tools that produce a *static* artifact (SVG/HTML/Markdown)

- **lowlighter/metrics** — GitHub Action that renders static SVG panels committed to your repo/README. It fetches via the API, so you can scope to owned repos and commit activity rather than stars. https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics
- **Ashutosh00710/github-readme-activity-graph** — generates a static activity/commit graph image. https://github.com/Ashutosh00710/github-readme-activity-graph
- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — Action that writes your recent authored activity (PushEvents/commits) as static Markdown into a README. https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme
- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — static SVG cards; the stats card counts commits/contributions and you can exclude forked/starred noise via `exclude_repo` and `count_private`. https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats

## If you want a self-hosted static "log" page
- **git-quick-stats** — shell tool that produces per-author commit reports you can render/export statically. https://github.com/arzzen/git-quick-stats
- **git-of-theseus** / **git-history (simonw)** — build static datasets/pages from a repo's commit history for authored analysis:
  - https://github.com/erikbern/git-of-theseus
  - https://github.com/simonw/git-history

## Recommended path
For a public, static, no-server build log scoped to authored commits: use **lowlighter/metrics** (most configurable, fetches owned repos + commit activity and outputs committed SVG), or roll your own static page that calls `/search/commits?q=author:{login}` at build time. Both cleanly avoid stars and bookmark-forks by construction.

I don't have private details on any specific instance you may already run — these are the public primary sources.

## Short answer

I can't point to a well-known, verifiable roster of *individual developer portfolios* that publish **both** an `llms.txt` **and** a bespoke JSON "project manifest for agents." That specific combo isn't (yet) an established convention, so naming particular personal sites would risk fabrication. What I *can* ground in public sources are the building blocks people combine to do exactly this, plus adjacent real conventions.

## The standards you'd actually assemble

**`llms.txt`** — the primary spec, from Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI. A Markdown file at site root giving LLMs a curated map of your content.
- Spec: https://llmstxt.org/
- Proposal repo: https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt
- Directory of sites that publish one (search here for real examples, including dev sites): https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/ and https://llmstxt.site/

**JSON manifest side** — there isn't a single "agent project manifest" standard, so people reuse existing JSON conventions:
- **schema.org `SoftwareSourceCode` / `CreativeWork`** as JSON-LD embedded in portfolio pages — the closest thing to a machine-readable "project manifest." Docs: https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode
- **`.well-known/` URIs** (RFC 8615) as the conventional home for machine-readable metadata: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615
- **Agent-oriented well-known files** now emerging:
  - `ai-plugin.json` (OpenAI plugin manifest, the original "manifest for agents" pattern): https://platform.openai.com/docs/plugins/getting-started
  - `agents.json` from Wildcard AI — a JSON spec layering agent-executable actions over an OpenAPI file: https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json
  - `AGENTS.md` (Markdown, not JSON, but the dominant "instructions for coding agents" convention now): https://agents.md/ and https://github.com/openai/agents.md

## Realistic patterns people publish today

- Portfolio/docs sites emitting `llms.txt` + `llms-full.txt` automatically — common in tooling like **Mintlify** (https://mintlify.com/docs/ai/llmstxt) and **Fern**, and via framework plugins such as the Next.js/Vite generators listed in the llms-txt repo's tooling section.
- JSON-LD `SoftwareSourceCode` blocks per project + an `llms.txt` index — a legitimate DIY combo, but I'd be inventing names to attribute it to specific individuals.

## Niche OSS to build it

- `llmstxt` generators (see the "Tools and software" section of https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt)
- `llms_txt2ctx` CLI (parses llms.txt into an LLM context): https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt (same repo, `/llms_txt` package)
- `firecrawl`'s llms.txt generator: https://github.com/mendableai/firecrawl

## Honest gap

If you have a *specific* site in mind that does the exact `llms.txt` + JSON-manifest pairing, share the URL and I'll analyze it. Otherwise, the truthful state of the public web is: the `llms.txt` half is a real, adopted convention with a public directory; the "JSON project manifest for agents" half is still fragmented across `ai-plugin.json`, `agents.json`, and schema.org JSON-LD — and I won't manufacture named portfolios claiming to combine them.

TUI frameworks + ready-made cockpit references.

**TUI frameworks**

- Bubble Tea + Bubbles/Lip Gloss (Go) — Elm-arch TUI, strong widget set: https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea

results.stdout:
**Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta** — a solid 20-minute weeknight one.

## Ingredients (serves 2–3)
- 250g pasta (penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti)
- 2 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 250g mushrooms (cremini/button), sliced
- 2–3 cloves garlic, minced
- 150g fresh spinach
- 150ml cream (or half-and-half; splash of pasta water to loosen)
- 50g grated Parmesan
- Salt, pepper, pinch of chili flakes; optional squeeze of lemon

## Method
1. Boil pasta in salted water. **Reserve a cup of pasta water** before draining.
2. Heat oil + butter over medium-high. Add mushrooms, spread out, and let them sit ~3–4 min before stirring so they brown (don't crowd or they steam). Season with salt.
3. Add garlic (and chili flakes), cook ~30 sec until fragrant.
4. Add spinach in handfuls; stir until wilted (~1–2 min).
5. Lower heat, pour in cream, simmer 2 min. Stir in Parmesan.
6. Toss in drained pasta with a splash of pasta water until glossy. Adjust salt/pepper, finish with lemon.

**Tips:** Dry mushrooms well and salt them *after* browning. Vegan swap: olive oil + coconut/oat cream + nutritional yeast. Add protein with white beans or shredded rotisserie chicken.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source market splits into two camps: frameworks that coordinate agents, and SDLC control planes that connect agent work to branches, PRs, CI, review, and auditable artifacts. For “evidence-based shipping,” the second group is more relevant.

## Strongest matches

| Project / shipper | What it publicly ships | Evidence and delivery model | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Agent Orchestrator — Untrivial AI](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator) | Apache-2.0 control plane for parallel Codex, Claude Code, Aider, OpenCode, Cursor, and other coding agents | Isolated worktrees; PR awareness; CI failures, review comments, and merge conflicts routed back to the responsible agent; reviewer-agent loop; visible session state | Probably the closest open-source match to a practical multi-agent software factory |
| [GitHub Agentic Workflows (`gh-aw`)](https://github.com/github/gh-aw) | MIT-licensed natural-language workflows compiled into GitHub Actions | Committed workflow source and generated lock file, Actions logs, issues/PRs as outputs, permission controls, sandboxing, human approval gates, tracker IDs and safe-output sanitization | Strongest repository-native audit trail and governance; less of a standalone “agent team” |
| [MetaSwarm — Dave Sifry](https://github.com/dsifry/metaswarm) | Multi-agent SDLC workflow for Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and OpenCode | Spec-driven development, TDD enforcement, coverage thresholds, parallel review gates, PR/CI lifecycle automation, git-native knowledge records | Very explicit about quality gates and lifecycle evidence, but newer and less proven than the leading platforms |
| [Kandev](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev) | AGPL self-hosted workbench for multiple coding-agent providers | Tasks, isolated workspaces, diffs, reviews, PR creation, remote runtimes and agent-session history | Strong operator UX and self-hosting; evidence policy is largely supplied by your repo and CI |
| [Sudocode](https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode) | Lightweight, repository-local orchestration around specs, issues, task DAGs and coding agents | Persistent task graph and context, parallel worktrees, dependency-aware execution | Interesting niche choice when you want planning provenance in Git rather than a large control-plane product |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | MIT software-agent SDK, CLI and local GUI; agents can be composed and scaled | Sandboxed execution, event histories, tests, and separate public [benchmark infrastructure](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) supporting SWE-bench and other evaluations | Strongest general autonomous-development runtime and evaluation ecosystem; not primarily an issue-to-merge multi-agent coordinator |
| [GitHub SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Agent that converts GitHub issues into repository fixes | Reproducible trajectories and evaluation against executable tests/SWE-bench | Excellent research baseline and worker agent; orchestration across a complete SDLC needs another layer |

My first evaluation stack would be Agent Orchestrator for local, heterogeneous agent fleets, or `gh-aw` when GitHub Actions is the desired system of record. MetaSwarm is the sharper experimental candidate if mandatory TDD and multiple review gates are central.

## Earlier “virtual software company” systems

These are genuinely multi-agent and software-specific, but their notion of completion tends to be weaker than PR/CI-backed shipping:

- [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) implements product-manager, architect, project-manager and engineer roles around explicit SOPs. It is useful for role-based planning and artifact generation.

- [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) originated as a virtual software company covering design, coding, testing and documentation; version 2 broadens this into a general configurable multi-agent platform.

They are useful research and prototyping systems. I would not treat an agent debate, generated document, or simulated QA role as production evidence unless it terminates in external tests, static analysis, deployment checks and a reviewable PR.

## General orchestration frameworks

These organizations ship credible public orchestration components, but not an autonomous SDLC out of the box:

- Microsoft: [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) — agent teams, event-driven messaging, tools and human intervention.
- LangChain: [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) — durable state graphs, checkpoints, interrupts and tracing.
- CrewAI: [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) — role-based crews and deterministic flows.
- OpenAI: [Swarm](https://github.com/openai/swarm) — educational handoff/orchestration patterns rather than a production SDLC platform.
- OpenBMB: ChatDev 2.0, noted above.
- Foundation Agents: MetaGPT, noted above.

These are appropriate if you want to design your own planner–implementer–reviewer–tester topology. You must build worktree isolation, retries, CI ingestion, merge rules, provenance and authorization yourself.

## Evidence layer worth combining with orchestration

Several open-source projects cover the verification half better than most orchestrators:

- [Continue](https://github.com/continuedev/continue) stores AI checks in `.continue/checks/` and runs them as enforceable PR status checks. This is a particularly clean example of source-controlled agent policy.

- [PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) provides automated PR descriptions, reviews and improvement suggestions through GitHub Actions or a CLI. Note that the repository describes itself as a community-maintained legacy project distinct from Qodo’s current commercial product.

- [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench) supplies executable, real-world issue-resolution evaluation instead of relying on subjective agent judgments.

- [OpenHands Benchmarks](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) provides standardized pipelines for SWE-bench, Commit0 and safety evaluations.

- [Kodus Agent Readiness](https://github.com/kodustech/agent-readiness) assesses whether a repository has the documentation, tests and CI structure needed for autonomous agents, with CI thresholds.

## What “evidence-based shipping” should mean

A credible platform should leave machine-verifiable records for:

1. Requirement and acceptance criteria.
2. Agent assignment and dependency graph.
3. Isolated branch or worktree containing the exact change.
4. Test, lint, type-check, security and build results tied to the commit SHA.
5. Reviewer findings and their resolution.
6. Preview/deployment validation when applicable.
7. Human approval or an explicit policy authorizing autonomous merge.
8. Final PR, commit and deployment provenance.

Very few open-source projects deliver all eight cohesively. Today, the most defensible architecture is an SDLC orchestrator such as Agent Orchestrator, `gh-aw`, MetaSwarm or Kandev, backed by ordinary deterministic CI and an evidence layer such as Continue checks—not a collection of LLM agents voting that their own work is correct.

## Earlier “virtual software company” systems

These are genuinely multi-agent and software-specific, but their notion of completion tends to be weaker than PR/CI-backed shipping:

- [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) implements product-manager, architect, project-manager and engineer roles around explicit SOPs. It is useful for role-based planning and artifact generation.

- [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) originated as a virtual software company covering design, coding, testing and documentation; version 2 broadens this into a general configurable multi-agent platform.

They are useful research and prototyping systems. I would not treat an agent debate, generated document, or simulated QA role as production evidence unless it terminates in external tests, static analysis, deployment checks and a reviewable PR.

## General orchestration frameworks

These organizations ship credible public orchestration components, but not an autonomous SDLC out of the box:

- Microsoft: [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) — agent teams, event-driven messaging, tools and human intervention.
- LangChain: [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) — durable state graphs, checkpoints, interrupts and tracing.
- CrewAI: [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) — role-based crews and deterministic flows.
- OpenAI: [Swarm](https://github.com/openai/swarm) — educational handoff/orchestration patterns rather than a production SDLC platform.
- OpenBMB: ChatDev 2.0, noted above.
- Foundation Agents: MetaGPT, noted above.

These are appropriate if you want to design your own planner–implementer–reviewer–tester topology. You must build worktree isolation, retries, CI ingestion, merge rules, provenance and authorization yourself.

Several open-source projects cover the verification half better than most orchestrators:

- [Continue](https://github.com/continuedev/continue) stores AI checks in `.continue/checks/` and runs them as enforceable PR status checks. This is a particularly clean example of source-controlled agent policy.

- [PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) provides automated PR descriptions, reviews and improvement suggestions through GitHub Actions or a CLI. Note that the repository describes itself as a community-maintained legacy project distinct from Qodo’s current commercial product.

- [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench) supplies executable, real-world issue-resolution evaluation instead of relying on subjective agent judgments.

- [OpenHands Benchmarks](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) provides standardized pipelines for SWE-bench, Commit0 and safety evaluations.

- [Kodus Agent Readiness](https://github.com/kodustech/agent-readiness) assesses whether a repository has the documentation, tests and CI structure needed for autonomous agents, with CI thresholds.

A credible platform should leave machine-verifiable records for:

1. Requirement and acceptance criteria.
2. Agent assignment and dependency graph.
3. Isolated branch or worktree containing the exact change.
4. Test, lint, type-check, security and build results tied to the commit SHA.
5. Reviewer findings and their resolution.
6. Preview/deployment validation when applicable.
7. Human approval or an explicit policy authorizing autonomous merge.
8. Final PR, commit and deployment provenance.

Very few open-source projects deliver all eight cohesively. Today, the most defensible architecture is an SDLC orchestrator such as Agent Orchestrator, `gh-aw`, MetaSwarm or Kandev, backed by ordinary deterministic CI and an evidence layer such as Continue checks—not a collection of LLM agents voting that their own work is correct.

Yes—assuming “zero-daemon” means no additional service beyond tmux’s own server.

The closest match is [eduwass/tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Raycast-style palette inside a tmux popup.
- Invoked on demand from a tmux key binding; it exits after dispatching the selection.
- Harness-neutral: actions are arbitrary shell or tmux commands, so Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Aider, or custom wrappers work equally well.
- Can launch agents in new panes using the current pane’s working directory.
- Configuration is local JSON.
- Small, MIT-licensed codebase with no runtime package dependencies, although it requires Bun and recommends tmux 3.4+.

For example, its `commands.json` could contain:

```json
[
  {
    "title": "New Codex pane",
    "category": "Agents",
    "action": {
      "tmux": "split-window -h -c '#{pane_current_path}' codex"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "New Claude pane",
    "category": "Agents",
    "action": {
      "tmux": "split-window -h -c '#{pane_current_path}' claude"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "New OpenCode pane",
    "category": "Agents",
    "action": {
      "tmux": "split-window -v -c '#{pane_current_path}' opencode"
    }
  }
]
```

Its documented action model supports direct tmux commands, ordinary shell commands, popups, and nested palettes. Dynamic palettes can also be generated by any command that prints JSON or newline-separated items.

The caveat is that `tmux-palette` is a general tmux command palette, not an agent-aware control plane. It launches and navigates panes but does not inherently understand whether an agent is working, waiting for approval, or finished.

If you want more orchestration:

- [standardagents/dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) offers an agent chooser, multiple agent CLIs, tmux panes, and isolated Git worktrees. It is closer to a full workspace manager than a global command palette.
- [raine/workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) supports configurable pane layouts and Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode, Kiro, Pi, and custom commands. It is especially good when every task should receive a branch/worktree.
- [Agent of Empires](https://github.com/agent-of-empires/agent-of-empires) is highly harness-neutral and tmux-based, but it is a persistent session-management TUI rather than a lightweight palette.
- [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck) supports multiple harnesses and richer monitoring, but its optional integrations include a bridge daemon, so it is not the cleanest fit for a strict zero-daemon requirement.

Bottom line: `tmux-palette` is the best literal match, provided you are happy to define the agent-launch entries yourself. `dmux` is the better choice when “run agents” also implies worktree creation, status, merging, and lifecycle management.

There are strong public analogues, but I couldn’t find a genuinely public, interactive twin of a multi-floor padel/tennis/pickleball facility with live autonomous operations. Most deployed twins remain private because they expose building systems, security, and operational data.

The best references are:

| Reference | Public material | Why it matches |
|---|---|---|
| OnePlan VenueTwin / Paris 2024 | [VenueTwin overview](https://www.oneplan.io/venue-twin/), [Eiffel Tower Arena demo video](https://vimeo.com/849513374), [Aquatics Centre demo](https://vimeo.com/947019909) | Probably the closest visual precedent. It supports detailed indoor spaces across floor levels, event configurations, field-of-play planning, broadcast positions, and crowd/operations workflows. Public videos, but the interactive twins require a demo/account. |
| SoFi Stadium + Willow | [Official case announcement](https://www.sofistadium.com/news/detail/willow-to-deliver-digital-twin-technology-solutions-at-new-sofi-stadium-and-hollywood-park), [demo video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iPKlNMy23rk), [technical case study](https://www.enr.com/articles/50568-sofi-stadium-builds-out-digital-twin-for-operations-and-maintenance) | A real operational twin of a 3.1-million-square-foot, deeply multi-level facility. It connects BIM, live building systems, maintenance data, lighting, HVAC, and roughly 136,000 assets. Excellent model for a large autonomous venue, although the actual twin is private. |
| Nissan Stadium pedestrian twin | [InControl case-study PDF](https://www.incontrolsim.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Sports-Entertainment-Digital-Twin-Application.pdf) | Particularly relevant for simulating movement between floors, court turnover, emergency egress, queues, and occupancy. The demonstrated use case models every seat and shelter route. |
| Munich Olympic Stadium roof twin | [ASHVIN Demo Site #9](https://www.ashvin.eu/2023/05/18/ashvin-demo-site-9-sports-stadium-roof-structure-support-to-asset-maintenance-with-digital-twins/) | A public EU research demonstration connecting structural sensors, inspection, maintenance, BIM, and simulation. Narrower than a whole venue, but more technically transparent than most commercial case studies. |
| Autodesk Tandem | [Interactive-twin product and free tier](https://www.autodesk.com/products/tandem/overview), [workflow walkthrough](https://intandem.autodesk.com/explore-autodesk-tandem/), [UI documentation](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/ENU/Tandem-Getting-Started/files/tandem-navigate-ui.html) | The easiest general-purpose reference for prototyping a multi-floor BIM twin with rooms, court equipment, HVAC, access systems, historical telemetry, and heatmaps. It is not sports-specific. |
| PathRa | [Browser demo and product page](https://pathra.world/) | A lighter, public-facing venue twin built from drone capture and Gaussian splatting. Useful for customer navigation and sales previews, but not yet a deep operational twin. |

For autonomous racket-sports operations, these are the closest deployed public examples:

- [Smart Padel House](https://www.smartpadelhouse.com/) demonstrates a 24/7 automated padel facility with app/biometric entry, booking, payment, and private spaces.
- [Doinsport autonomous courts](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts) shows the operational sequence clearly: reservation, temporary access credential, remote unlocking, and automatically scheduled lighting.
- [PSC Club](https://www.psccourts.com/en/psc-club-en/) combines automated processes with smart lighting, court-wide cameras, displays, sound, streaming, and match statistics.
- [SportReTiNA](https://sportretina.com/) is a relevant smart-court layer for tennis and padel, centered on installed court cameras and analytics.
- [VenueTwin’s multi-floor description](https://www.venuetwin.com/any-venue/) explicitly covers navigating and managing every internal floor level, making it the strongest bridge between these automated club systems and a spatial twin.

These autonomous-club examples are not full digital twins by themselves. They are the physical and operational systems a real facility twin would need to represent.

For an open-source demonstrator, I’d combine:

- [xeokit SDK](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk) and its [live BIM examples](https://xeokit.github.io/xeokit-sdk/examples/index.html) for multi-floor IFC/BIM rendering, object selection, slicing, measurements, and floor isolation.
- [Eclipse Ditto](https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto) and its [live Explorer UI](https://eclipse-ditto.github.io/ditto/) for the digital state of doors, lights, lockers, cameras, ball machines, HVAC zones, and court occupancy.
- [OpenRemote](https://openremote.io/product/) for open-source automation, floor plans, access control, rules, alarms, and live asset locations.
- [DT3D for Home Assistant](https://github.com/tentone/dt3d-ha), a very niche but relevant example of binding editable 3D rooms and real sensor states. It is residential, but the interaction pattern transfers cleanly to courts and club floors.

A convincing racket-facility demo would model three synchronized layers:

1. The building: floors, courts, stairs, lifts, plant rooms and evacuation paths.
2. Operations: bookings, QR access, lighting, occupancy, cleaning and court status.
3. Autonomous equipment: cameras, ball machines, delivery/cleaning robots and fault states.

The most useful visual benchmark is OnePlan; the strongest operational benchmark is SoFi/Willow; and the most practical open-source prototype path is xeokit + Eclipse Ditto or OpenRemote.

For autonomous racket-sports operations, these are the closest deployed public examples:

- [Smart Padel House](https://www.smartpadelhouse.com/) demonstrates a 24/7 automated padel facility with app/biometric entry, booking, payment, and private spaces.
- [Doinsport autonomous courts](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts) shows the operational sequence clearly: reservation, temporary access credential, remote unlocking, and automatically scheduled lighting.
- [PSC Club](https://www.psccourts.com/en/psc-club-en/) combines automated processes with smart lighting, court-wide cameras, displays, sound, streaming, and match statistics.
- [SportReTiNA](https://sportretina.com/) is a relevant smart-court layer for tennis and padel, centered on installed court cameras and analytics.
- [VenueTwin’s multi-floor description](https://www.venuetwin.com/any-venue/) explicitly covers navigating and managing every internal floor level, making it the strongest bridge between these automated club systems and a spatial twin.

These autonomous-club examples are not full digital twins by themselves. They are the physical and operational systems a real facility twin would need to represent.

For an open-source demonstrator, I’d combine:

- [xeokit SDK](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk) and its [live BIM examples](https://xeokit.github.io/xeokit-sdk/examples/index.html) for multi-floor IFC/BIM rendering, object selection, slicing, measurements, and floor isolation.

- [OpenRemote](https://openremote.io/product/) for open-source automation, floor plans, access control, rules, alarms, and live asset locations.
- [DT3D for Home Assistant](https://github.com/tentone/dt3d-ha), a very niche but relevant example of binding editable 3D rooms and real sensor states. It is residential, but the interaction pattern transfers cleanly to courts and club floors.

A convincing racket-facility demo would model three synchronized layers:

1. The building: floors, courts, stairs, lifts, plant rooms and evacuation paths.
2. Operations: bookings, QR access, lighting, occupancy, cleaning and court status.
3. Autonomous equipment: cameras, ball machines, delivery/cleaning robots and fault states.

The most useful visual benchmark is OnePlan; the strongest operational benchmark is SoFi/Willow; and the most practical open-source prototype path is xeokit + Eclipse Ditto or OpenRemote.
