The closest ready-made option is [Commits.site](https://www.commits.site/), an open-source dashboard that ranks repositories by your actual commit counts. Its source is [HelgeSverre/contribution-overview](https://github.com/HelgeSverre/contribution-overview). It does not treat stars as work, though its hosted dashboard is client-side rather than a permanently published static profile.

For a precise, immediately shareable authored-commit log, GitHub’s native commit search is the authoritative option:

```text
https://github.com/search?q=author%3AYOUR_USERNAME&type=commits&s=committer-date&o=desc
```

The `author:USERNAME` qualifier filters on commit authorship; GitHub documents it in [Searching commits](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits), and the equivalent CLI is [`gh search commits --author USERNAME`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits). Repositories that you merely starred or forked without authoring a commit will not appear. The downside is that this is a search-results page, not a polished static build log.

Other useful options:

- [GitShow](https://gitshow.dev/) gives every public username a shareable page at `gitshow.dev/USERNAME` and highlights commits and PRs to external repositories. Its source is linked from the site. It is a polished public portfolio, but not strictly commits-only.
- [gitbox](https://gitbox.app/) visualizes public commit history by repository without requiring login. It is closer to a contribution diary than a repository build log.
- GitHub’s own profile activity is public, but it is not strict enough: GitHub counts repository creation, forks, issues, PRs, reviews, and qualifying commits as contributions, as explained in its [profile contributions reference](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

If “static” is a hard requirement, there does not appear to be a well-established hosted service that is simultaneously static, public, repository-grouped, and strictly authored-commit-only. The robust solution is a small GitHub Pages site regenerated on a schedule:

1. Fetch `author:USERNAME` results through GitHub’s commit search API/CLI.
2. Deduplicate by repository and commit SHA.
3. Generate plain HTML/JSON.
4. Publish through GitHub Actions and Pages, which officially supports [custom static build workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site).

That approach also lets you explicitly exclude unchanged forks while retaining forks in which you authored real commits.

The closest ready-made option is [Commits.site](https://www.commits.site/), an open-source dashboard that ranks repositories by your actual commit counts. Its source is [HelgeSverre/contribution-overview](https://github.com/HelgeSverre/contribution-overview). It does not treat stars as work, though its hosted dashboard is client-side rather than a permanently published static profile.

For a precise, immediately shareable authored-commit log, GitHub’s native commit search is the authoritative option:

```text
https://github.com/search?q=author%3AYOUR_USERNAME&type=commits&s=committer-date&o=desc
```

The `author:USERNAME` qualifier filters on commit authorship; GitHub documents it in [Searching commits](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits), and the equivalent CLI is [`gh search commits --author USERNAME`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits). Repositories that you merely starred or forked without authoring a commit will not appear. The downside is that this is a search-results page, not a polished static build log.

Other useful options:

- [GitShow](https://gitshow.dev/) gives every public username a shareable page at `gitshow.dev/USERNAME` and highlights commits and PRs to external repositories. Its source is linked from the site. It is a polished public portfolio, but not strictly commits-only.
- [gitbox](https://gitbox.app/) visualizes public commit history by repository without requiring login. It is closer to a contribution diary than a repository build log.
- GitHub’s own profile activity is public, but it is not strict enough: GitHub counts repository creation, forks, issues, PRs, reviews, and qualifying commits as contributions, as explained in its [profile contributions reference](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

If “static” is a hard requirement, there does not appear to be a well-established hosted service that is simultaneously static, public, repository-grouped, and strictly authored-commit-only. The robust solution is a small GitHub Pages site regenerated on a schedule:

1. Fetch `author:USERNAME` results through GitHub’s commit search API/CLI.
2. Deduplicate by repository and commit SHA.
3. Generate plain HTML/JSON.
4. Publish through GitHub Actions and Pages, which officially supports [custom static build workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site).

That approach also lets you explicitly exclude unchanged forks while retaining forks in which you authored real commits.

- **Doug Finke** — [portfolio](https://dougfinke.dev/), [`llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt), [`projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json). The visible portfolio explicitly directs agents to these two structured-context endpoints.

- **Prasad Gade** — [portfolio](https://prasadgade.dev/), [`llms.txt`](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt), [`projects.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json). This is the most extensive example: it also publishes a [structured résumé](https://prasadgade.dev/api/resume.json), [skills](https://prasadgade.dev/api/skills.json), [agent card](https://prasadgade.dev/.well-known/agent.json), and [OpenAPI document](https://prasadgade.dev/openapi.json).

- **Arnau Encina Salvà** — [portfolio](https://arnauencina.vercel.app/), [`llms.txt`](https://arnauencina.vercel.app/llms.txt), [`portfolio.json`](https://arnauencina.vercel.app/api/portfolio.json). He publicly describes the pairing as a portfolio designed for human and agent consumption in his [launch post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/arnau-encina_avui-publico-el-meu-portfolio-personal-activity-7458070835417919488-S09F).

- **Cuttle / 0xCuttlefish** — [portfolio ecosystem](https://cuttle.af/), [`llms.txt`](https://cuttle.af/llms.txt), [`portfolio.json`](https://cuttle.af/portfolio.json). This is an unusual multi-domain developer/creator portfolio: its [documentation](https://blog.cuttle.af/about/) says the manifest connects eight domains and related concepts. The companion implementation is published at [agent-native-content](https://git.cuttle.af/cuttle/agent-native-content).

Adjacent but not strictly personal portfolios:

- **Buffalo Projects** publishes individual builder records as an agent-readable “JSON twin,” alongside `llms.txt` and `project.md`; see its [developer-facing overview](https://buffaloprojects.com/).

- **PalatineAI** pairs [`llms.txt`](https://palatineai.site/llms.txt) with a substantial [`projects.json`](https://palatineai.site/projects.json), though it is a ranked project-research portfolio rather than one developer’s résumé.

One important caveat: [`llms.txt`](https://llmstxt.org/) has a proposed common format, but `projects.json`/`portfolio.json` does not. Each example has invented its own schema. If building this pattern, I’d use `/llms.txt` for discovery and `/projects.json` for stable structured records, publish a JSON Schema URL/version inside the manifest, and link the JSON endpoint from `llms.txt`.

Yes. I’d build this as three composable layers sharing one event and identity model, rather than adopting one large “agent company” platform.

## 1. Company issue graph

Model operational work as a property graph:

- Nodes: `Company`, `Team`, `Person`, `Service`, `Repository`, `Issue`, `PR`, `Incident`, `Decision`, `AgentRun`, `Artifact`
- Edges: `OWNS`, `BLOCKS`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `DEPENDS_ON`, `CAUSED_BY`, `DECIDED_IN`, `ASSIGNED_TO`, `PRODUCED`

Every edge should carry `source_url`, `observed_at`, `confidence`, and `source_revision`. That provenance is crucial when agents consume the graph.

Recommended components:

- [Apache AGE](https://age.apache.org/) — graph queries inside PostgreSQL. This is my default because tickets, permissions, audit records, and event cursors remain comfortable relational data while dependencies use Cypher-style traversal.
- [Cytoscape.js](https://js.cytoscape.org/) — mature MIT-licensed interactive graph visualization with layouts, filtering, serialization, and built-in graph algorithms.
- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) — open-source Jira/Linear-style issue tracker if you need the source-of-truth UI too.
- [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) — broader open-source workspace spanning project management, communication, and documents.
- Native source APIs and webhooks: [GitHub’s issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) already expose blocking relationships through the CLI/API.

Do not make the visual graph itself authoritative. Keep source IDs such as `github:org/repo#123`, normalize them into graph entities, and retain raw source events for replay.

## 2. Agent harness contracts

Use small, versioned JSON Schema contracts rather than encoding execution semantics in prompts:

```text
TaskContract
  objective, inputs, allowed_tools, write_scopes
  budgets, approval_policy, acceptance_tests

RunEvent
  run_id, task_id, sequence, timestamp
  status, actor, tool_call, artifact_refs, trace_id

RunResult
  outcome, evidence, changed_resources
  verification_results, unresolved_risks
```

Use existing public protocols around those domain contracts:

- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for typed tools, resources, and prompts.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when independently deployed agents must discover and delegate to one another.
- [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com/) for streaming agent state and interaction events to the cockpit.
- [OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/registry/attributes/gen-ai/) for trace correlation rather than inventing proprietary observability fields.
- [Open Policy Agent](https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa) for deterministic authorization over tool calls, repositories, environments, and approval requirements.
- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) for reproducible harness and agent evaluations.

The core rule: the model proposes actions; ordinary code validates contracts, enforces policy, executes tools, records effects, and verifies completion.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

The cockpit should consume structured `RunEvent`s—not infer state by scraping colored terminal output.

Strong existing projects:

- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx) — closest match to a project cockpit: tasks, multiple coding-agent sessions, embedded tmux views, orchestration, and an MCP server exposing its board.
- [Agent of Empires](https://github.com/agent-of-empires/agent-of-empires) — multi-agent TUI/web manager with branch isolation and optional Docker sandboxing.
- [agent-session-manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) — smaller Go/Bubble Tea manager for multiple agent CLIs organized by project.
- [ccboard](https://github.com/florianbruniaux/ccboard) — useful reference for session trees, activity, budgets, configuration, and cost views.
- [Zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) — solid terminal-workspace substrate if you want to build the cockpit rather than inherit another project’s workflow.

A useful cockpit layout would be:

```text
Projects/issues | Active runs and approvals | Selected run terminal
Graph blockers  | Tests, CI, diffs, budgets | Evidence and artifacts
```

## Recommended first implementation

I would start with:

- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE
- Cytoscape.js graph view
- MCP + JSON Schema task/result contracts
- OPA policy checks
- OpenTelemetry event traces
- agtx or Zellij as the cockpit substrate
- Git worktrees per modifying agent run

The most important integration object is a stable `task_id` shared by the issue graph, agent contract, Git branch/worktree, telemetry trace, terminal session, PR, and produced artifacts. That single join key turns three separate tools into an operational system.

Yes. I’d build this as three composable layers sharing one event and identity model, rather than adopting one large “agent company” platform.

## 1. Company issue graph

Model operational work as a property graph:

- Nodes: `Company`, `Team`, `Person`, `Service`, `Repository`, `Issue`, `PR`, `Incident`, `Decision`, `AgentRun`, `Artifact`
- Edges: `OWNS`, `BLOCKS`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `DEPENDS_ON`, `CAUSED_BY`, `DECIDED_IN`, `ASSIGNED_TO`, `PRODUCED`

Every edge should carry `source_url`, `observed_at`, `confidence`, and `source_revision`. That provenance is crucial when agents consume the graph.

Recommended components:

- [Apache AGE](https://age.apache.org/) — graph queries inside PostgreSQL. This is my default because tickets, permissions, audit records, and event cursors remain comfortable relational data while dependencies use Cypher-style traversal.
- [Cytoscape.js](https://js.cytoscape.org/) — mature MIT-licensed interactive graph visualization with layouts, filtering, serialization, and built-in graph algorithms.
- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) — open-source Jira/Linear-style issue tracker if you need the source-of-truth UI too.
- [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) — broader open-source workspace spanning project management, communication, and documents.
- Native source APIs and webhooks: [GitHub’s issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) already expose blocking relationships through the CLI/API.

Do not make the visual graph itself authoritative. Keep source IDs such as `github:org/repo#123`, normalize them into graph entities, and retain raw source events for replay.

## 2. Agent harness contracts

Use small, versioned JSON Schema contracts rather than encoding execution semantics in prompts:

```text
TaskContract
  objective, inputs, allowed_tools, write_scopes
  budgets, approval_policy, acceptance_tests

RunEvent
  run_id, task_id, sequence, timestamp
  status, actor, tool_call, artifact_refs, trace_id

RunResult
  outcome, evidence, changed_resources
  verification_results, unresolved_risks
```

Use existing public protocols around those domain contracts:

- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for typed tools, resources, and prompts.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when independently deployed agents must discover and delegate to one another.
- [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com/) for streaming agent state and interaction events to the cockpit.
- [OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/registry/attributes/gen-ai/) for trace correlation rather than inventing proprietary observability fields.
- [Open Policy Agent](https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa) for deterministic authorization over tool calls, repositories, environments, and approval requirements.
- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) for reproducible harness and agent evaluations.

The core rule: the model proposes actions; ordinary code validates contracts, enforces policy, executes tools, records effects, and verifies completion.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

The cockpit should consume structured `RunEvent`s—not infer state by scraping colored terminal output.

Strong existing projects:

- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx) — closest match to a project cockpit: tasks, multiple coding-agent sessions, embedded tmux views, orchestration, and an MCP server exposing its board.
- [Agent of Empires](https://github.com/agent-of-empires/agent-of-empires) — multi-agent TUI/web manager with branch isolation and optional Docker sandboxing.
- [agent-session-manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) — smaller Go/Bubble Tea manager for multiple agent CLIs organized by project.
- [ccboard](https://github.com/florianbruniaux/ccboard) — useful reference for session trees, activity, budgets, configuration, and cost views.
- [Zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) — solid terminal-workspace substrate if you want to build the cockpit rather than inherit another project’s workflow.

A useful cockpit layout would be:

```text
Projects/issues | Active runs and approvals | Selected run terminal
Graph blockers  | Tests, CI, diffs, budgets | Evidence and artifacts
```

## Recommended first implementation

I would start with:

- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE
- Cytoscape.js graph view
- MCP + JSON Schema task/result contracts
- OPA policy checks
- OpenTelemetry event traces
- agtx or Zellij as the cockpit substrate
- Git worktrees per modifying agent run

The most important integration object is a stable `task_id` shared by the issue graph, agent contract, Git branch/worktree, telemetry trace, terminal session, PR, and produced artifacts. That single join key turns three separate tools into an operational system.

For most independent dental clinics in 2026, **RevenueWell is the best overall dental CRM/patient-engagement platform**. If online scheduling and front-office automation matter more than marketing, choose **NexHealth** instead.

“HIPAA-compliant” is not a government certification. Any vendor handling electronic protected health information should sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), and the clinic must configure and operate the system appropriately. [HHS cloud-computing guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) confirms that a BAA and the clinic’s own risk analysis are required.

| Product | Best for | Notable capabilities | Public HIPAA evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RevenueWell** | Best overall for independent dental practices | Recall/reactivation, campaigns, two-way texting, reviews, forms, scheduling, payments, patient portal; integrates with Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Denticon and WinOMS | Documents encrypted PMS data transfer, HIPAA/HITECH safeguards and audits; its current AI documentation explicitly says it signs BAAs. [Platform](https://www.revenuewell.com/) · [HIPAA documentation](https://www.revenuewell.com/hipaa-compliance) |
| **NexHealth** | Best front-office automation and online booking | Real-time scheduling, waitlists, recalls, forms, messaging, payments, insurance verification and treatment-plan follow-up; broad PMS/EHR connectivity | Public trust center lists HIPAA and SOC 2, though detailed reports may require access. [Platform](https://www.nexhealth.com/) · [Trust center](https://security.nexhealth.com/) · [Scheduling](https://www.nexhealth.com/features/scheduling) |
| **Weave** | Best integrated phones and communications | VoIP, texting, reviews, online scheduling, payments, email marketing and mobile access | Publishes its BAA directly and describes encrypted communications and access safeguards. Carefully review its permitted AI uses of PHI. [Dental platform](https://www.getweave.com/industry/dentistry/) · [BAA](https://www.getweave.com/legal/baa/) |
| **CareStack** | Best all-in-one replacement for CRM plus practice-management software | Clinical records, scheduling, billing, insurance, patient portal, campaigns, messaging, reporting and multi-location controls | States that it acts as a HIPAA Business Associate and provides job-based permissions, audit trails, encrypted communications, backups and recovery. [HIPAA controls](https://carestack.com/dental-software/features/hipaa-compliant) |
| **OpenEMR** | Best open-source foundation for a custom deployment | GPL-licensed EHR/practice management, scheduling, billing, APIs and FHIR support | The project provides a HIPAA-oriented AWS deployment approach, but it is not dental-specific and compliance remains the operator’s responsibility. [GitHub](https://github.com/openemr/openemr) · [Project site](https://www.openemr.io/) |

### My practical picks

- **One or a few general-dentistry locations:** RevenueWell.
- **Modern booking, intake and automated front desk:** NexHealth.
- **Replacing phones as well as patient communications:** Weave.
- **Growing group or DSO that wants one operational system:** CareStack.
- **Custom/self-hosted project with dedicated security and IT staff:** OpenEMR—but it needs dental workflow development and should not be treated as turnkey HIPAA compliance.

Before signing, require written answers covering:

- A BAA for the exact subscription, integrations and AI features you will use.
- MFA, role-based permissions and immutable audit logs.
- Encryption in transit and at rest.
- Data export, deletion and retention after termination.
- Breach-notification deadlines and subcontractor responsibilities.
- Whether PHI, calls or transcripts train AI models.
- Direct compatibility with your exact Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, Denticon or other PMS version.
- Independent security evidence such as a current SOC 2 Type II report.

I would shortlist **RevenueWell, NexHealth and Weave**, then run demos using the same three workflows: new-patient booking, overdue hygiene recall and an unscheduled treatment plan. That comparison usually exposes the meaningful differences faster than feature checklists.

[GitHub](https://github.com/openemr/openemr) · [Project site](https://www.openemr.io/) |

### My practical picks

- **One or a few general-dentistry locations:** RevenueWell.
- **Modern booking, intake and automated front desk:** NexHealth.
- **Replacing phones as well as patient communications:** Weave.
- **Growing group or DSO that wants one operational system:** CareStack.
- **Custom/self-hosted project with dedicated security and IT staff:** OpenEMR—but it needs dental workflow development and should not be treated as turnkey HIPAA compliance.

Before signing, require written answers covering:

- A BAA for the exact subscription, integrations and AI features you will use.
- MFA, role-based permissions and immutable audit logs.
- Encryption in transit and at rest.
- Data export, deletion and retention after termination.
- Breach-notification deadlines and subcontractor responsibilities.
- Whether PHI, calls or transcripts train AI models.
- Direct compatibility with your exact Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, Denticon or other PMS version.
- Independent security evidence such as a current SOC 2 Type II report.

I would shortlist **RevenueWell, NexHealth and Weave**, then run demos using the same three workflows: new-patient booking, overdue hygiene recall and an unscheduled treatment plan. That comparison usually exposes the meaningful differences faster than feature checklists.

## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about **25 minutes**; serves **2–3**.

### Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) pasta
- 8 oz (225 g) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- ½ cup heavy cream or half-and-half
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- ½ tsp Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: red-pepper flakes, lemon juice

### Method

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve **1 cup pasta water**, then drain.
2. Heat olive oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes; then season and sauté until browned, about 5 minutes total.
3. Add garlic, Italian seasoning, and optional pepper flakes. Cook for 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat. Stir in the cream and ¼ cup pasta water, then add the spinach and cook until wilted.
5. Add the pasta and Parmesan. Toss until glossy, adding more pasta water as needed.
6. Taste for salt and pepper. A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens everything.

For a lighter version, skip the cream and emulsify the Parmesan with about ¾ cup pasta water. White beans or shredded rotisserie chicken make easy protein additions.
